2.text: During the greater part of the summer the reindeer are much worried

3.text: by large and small mosquitoes, and still more by two kinds of reindeer-flies.

4.text: The first one (Œstrus tarandi Nordenskiöld, Tabanus tarandinus Slunin)
4.resolved: ö = o+U+0308 (Nordenskiöld, German surname, printed diaeresis)

5.text: lays its eggs on the hair of the reindeer, fastening them to the ends of the

6.text: hair. After a little while a small maggot hatches from the egg, and immedi-

7.text: ately makes its way into the epidermis. While there it grows rapidly, and

8.text: finally reaches the size of a hazel-nut. When full grown, it protrudes from

9.text: the skin, and is ready to fall down. The maggots evidently cause itching,

10.text: since the reindeer scratches its back whenever possible. When the maggots

11.text: are very numerous, the reindeer loses its fat, and sometimes even dies. Later

12.text: in spring the backs of some hapless animals look as if they were stuffed over

13.text: and over with maggots, and the skin is riddled with small holes. Chukchee

14.text: herdsmen very dexterously pick out these maggots, when large enough, from

15.text: the reindeer’s back, and eat them with great relish. The Lamut sometimes

16.text: gather a quantity and boil them in water. Although this fly, when laying its

17.text: eggs, does not cause the reindeer any pain or discomfort, the animal is much

18.text: more afraid of it than of the stinging mosquito, and the herd will not remain

19.text: quiet when the flies are numerous.

20.text: Another fly, of smaller size and darker color (Œdemagena tarandi Slunin),

21.text: lays its eggs in the reindeer’s nostrils. The larvæ go up to the throat, and

22.text: penetrate the cartilage. The next year, when the maggots are full-grown,

23.text: they cause a constant cough, which continues until the last one drops to the

24.text: ground. The Yukaghir and the Tungus, following the example of Yakut

25.text: cattle-breeders, try to protect their reindeer from obnoxious insects by a smudge

26.text: of smouldering dung, or of a fire covered with green leaves. But with the

27.text: wild and large herds of the Chukchee such fires are of little value, and not

28.text: without danger. Thus, some five years ago, Tungus herdsmen who were

29.text: tending the herd of a rich Chukchee on the Alaseya River tried to surround

30.text: it with fires, and finally burned the whole pasture, and injured half of the

32.text: Hoof-swelling is the most common of reindeer-diseases, and occurs almost

33.text: every year to a greater or less extent in most herds. It develops where the

34.text: animals walk on dry and hot ground. Large abscesses break out between

35.text: the joints of the foot. Sometimes the foot swells to the size of a child’s head.

36.text: The disease is catching, and is more dangerous in the mountains than on the

37.text: seacoast. The Chukchee believe that when an animal afflicted with hoof-disease

38.text: steps on the tracks of a healthy animal, it communicates the disease to the

39.text: latter. Therefore an infected herd sometimes finds trouble in moving about

40.text: the country. In an unfavorable summer a third or even half of the herd may

41.text: die of it; but usually the loss amounts to only a few score. The first cold

42.text: rapidly restores health to those that were not seriously affected. The symptom
